intro: Variation IV of Elgar’s “Enigma” Variations, Op. 36, marked Allegro di molto, is the shortest of the portraits and depicts William Meath Baker, squire of Hasfield. In the music, Baker’s brisk announcements are set as hard accents, and the variation ends with his hurried exit.

sections.label: Var 4 · “W.M.B.”, Allegro di molto
sections.mNote: Repeated accents in a fast Allegro di molto.

cues.title: Variation IV, “W.M.B.”
cues.text: The marking is Allegro di molto. Strings and woodwinds play short, heavily accented phrases, with horns, trumpets and timpani behind them. The variation is brief and moves quickly to its last chord.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 20–23, rehearsal figures 11–14: opening accents and the concise ending. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/1e/IMSLP23792-PMLP07276-Elgar_-_Enigma_Variations_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Baker’s carriage arrangements
cues.text: Baker had a house full of guests and carriages to arrange. He read out the day’s plans forcefully from a slip of paper, then hurried from the music room and banged the door by accident. Elgar put the guests’ teasing response in the middle of the variation.
cues.evidence: Elgar, My Friends Pictured Within (Novello), section IV: the paper, carriage arrangements, door and guests’ response in bars 15–24. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/06/IMSLP339677-SIBLEY1802.27173.6d2a-39087004945996text.pdf. Baker’s Hasfield home: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations

source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 20–23, rehearsal figures 11–14: Variation IV, W.M.B., marked Allegro di molto.

timeline.note: Strings and woodwinds begin with clipped accents, reinforced by horns, trumpets and timpani (p. 20).
First violins, violas, cellos and basses play running figures beneath the longer wind notes. Flutes and low brass join the exchange (pp. 20–21).
Oboes and clarinets play in short notes. Flute and violin flourishes break in while the other strings leave gaps (p. 22).
The full orchestra returns to the opening accents, now marked fff, and stops suddenly (pp. 22–23).

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
